doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Okay. Let’s talk… Well, let’s, let’s digress for one more moment since you mentioned moving guys out of the hotel…
Yeah.
…and it was crummy and… There’s obviously a business aspect to music. Not to the making of it but towards maybe the maintaining of it.
Yeah.
And at some point, and we’re about to talk about your compositions, but before we talk about the artist’s part of it…
Mm-hmm.
At some point, you started a publishing company. Do you remember how that came to be so that you could maintain control of your own works?
Oh, yeah. No, I don’t. Probably Jane would answer that better. Either that or Mary Ann Topper or Anna or something but…
Well, Janhall Music…
Oh, Janhall Music, that’s right. Dot-com. (laughs)
No, it’s not a dot-com but…
No, I’m kidding. You know I’m kidding, right?
Pre-dates them, actually.
Yeah.
And I was wondering if maybe John Lewis talked to you about it, because he had MJQ Music already.
Yeah. Yeah.
That some of your colleagues…

Oh, I guess, yeah. Yeah, it probably had to do with getting royalties from recordings and that sort of thing. And yeah, John might have advised me. “Dummy, you gotta,” you know, (laughs) “get a company.” And then… maybe the lawyer that we had… Noel Silverman?
Mm-hmm. Noel Silverman.
Yeah. I can’t remember that specifically, but, but it has come in handy and every once in a while I’ll get, as you know, get a nice royalty check so that’s worked out great. Thank you for that.
So that’s something you would advise young people who are beginning to think about composing and whatever to, to have an awareness of that or…?
I would think so just from a… It sounds rather unartistic, but it is necessary to eat, as well. Otherwise, it’s hard to write music if you’re starving to death. (laughs) So…
Well put.
Yeah.
